title: Lead me from the unreal
hookLine: the one thing the demons couldn't break, and the prayer that asks to be led from death to the deathless
carry: lead me from the unreal to the real
tomorrow: what does the Gita say to a day that stings?

cards: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad tells it like a contest. The gods and the asuras, the demons, both children of Prajapati, are fighting over the worlds. The gods decide to win with a sacred chant.
They ask speech to sing it, and the demons pierce speech with evil: that, the text says, is why we say what we shouldn't. They try smell, the eye, the ear, the mind. Each one is pierced.
Last, they ask the breath in the mouth. The demons rush at it, and shatter, like a clod of earth thrown against a rock.

teach.b: At the end of the same chapter, the Upanishad gives a chant. You may know it. Asato ma sad gamaya.
Tamaso ma jyotir gamaya. Mrityor ma amritam gamaya. Lead me from the unreal to the real.
From darkness to light. From death to the deathless. Then the Upanishad does something rare: it explains itself.

teach.h: UNREAL TO REAL. DARK TO LIGHT. DEATH TO THE DEATHLESS.
teach.b: The unreal is death; the real is the deathless.
Darkness is death; light is the deathless. All three lines ask for one thing. Many teachers hear the whole Hindu hope in it: moksha, freedom, the self led out of what dies into what doesn't.
Gamaya: make me go, lead me, from gam, to go. Sat, the real, from as, to be: the root of asti, is.

teach.h: LEAD ME TO WHAT TRULY IS.
teach.b: So the prayer asks to be led to what truly is. And notice the voice: lead me. Not "I'll get there."

Like Arjuna's "teach me," it's a seeker asking. That's why it's so often chanted at the start of study, at prayer time, and when a lamp is lit: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, from darkness to light, is the line the flame says.
So on a day when a phone, a mood, a plan all come and go, the prayer doesn't ask for more of them. It asks to be led toward what doesn't die.

how: Asato ma sad gamaya, from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, is chanted by many Hindus at the start of study, at prayer time and when a lamp is lit; the Upanishad itself explains the unreal as death and the real as the deathless.

o: the rules of a chanting contest
a spell to keep demons away
a prayer to be led from the unreal to the real

games.q: the prayer, word by word — tap the pairs.

s: in the story, speech is the one thing the demons couldn't pierce
speech, smell, eye, ear and mind were pierced. the breath in the mouth wasn't.
the Upanishad explains its own prayer: the unreal is death, the real is the deathless
all three lines ask for the same thing.
it means make me go, lead me: the seeker asks to be led.

games.q: your little cousin hears you say "tamaso ma jyotir gamaya" while lighting a diya and asks if it just means "turn on the lights." what do you say?
o: it asks to be led from darkness to light, and the text says that means from death to the deathless.
yes, it's an old way of asking for more lamps.
it's a chant to scare off demons in the dark.
games.why: the Upanishad explains it: darkness is death, light is the deathless. the lamp is a picture of that bigger going.

practice: If there's a lamp or a candle you can light safely, light it; if not, turn toward the brightest window near you. Breathe in slowly: the breath the demons couldn't break.

On three out-breaths, say the three lines, aloud or silently: from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to the deathless. If you don't pray, just watch the light for three breaths. Then rest.

wordCard.voice: Two hundred core words. Today, gamaya, lead me, from gam, to go, and sat, the real, from as, to be. One prayer: going, toward what is.

orig.note: Sanskrit: from the unreal, lead me to the real (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28).

carryVoice: Here's the line: lead me from the unreal to the real, the prayer the lamp says out loud. Go gently.
